methodological_rigor.justification: Retrospective single-center cohort of 138 advanced gastric cancer patients with clearly defined inclusion/exclusion criteria and blinded radiologist measurements (ICC 0.938). The authors used an internally derived optimal cutoff (14%) which risks overfitting, though they performed bootstrap and 5-fold cross-validation (optimism-corrected C-index 0.756) and sensitivity analyses for heterogeneous follow-up intervals. Lack of external validation, absence of a control group not receiving ICIs, and no immune profiling to substantiate mechanism weaken the inferences. Statistical treatment is competent with Cox models, RCS for nonlinearity, multiplicity of cutoffs for inflammatory markers, time-dependent ROC, calibration, and decision curve analysis.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Individual retrospective cohort study (Oxford LoE 2b). The proposed ΔSV marker is non-invasive and CT-based, offering plausible prognostic utility during combination chemo-immunotherapy. Authors appropriately note that the nomogram is intended for risk stratification and surveillance rather than directly guiding treatment changes. Without external/prospective validation and with correlative-only mechanistic claims, the translational path is plausible but not yet practice-informing.

reporting_quality.justification: As an observational cohort study STROBE applies; most core items (setting, participants, variables, statistical methods, participant flow, limitations) are reported. The paper includes inter-observer reproducibility, sensitivity analyses, and internal validation but does not explicitly reference STROBE or include a flow diagram in the text, and effect sizes are presented with CIs throughout. No explicit data availability statement is visible in the provided text, nor is code shared, limiting reproducibility. Power calculation is absent.

novelty_literature.justification: Authors claim first report of ΔSV prognostic associations in gastric cancer under chemo-ICI and situate findings alongside prior RCC, pancreatic, NSCLC, and colorectal studies (Aslan, Niogret, Castagnoli, Yang). The conceptual approach of splenic volume as an imaging biomarker of systemic immunity is well-established; this study extends it to a new tumor type. Contribution is a meaningful disease-specific extension rather than a first-in-class method or mechanism.

writing_presentation.justification: Manuscript is well organized with clearly structured methods, results, and discussion; figures and tables are logically referenced with adequate legends. Language is generally precise and the limitations section is thoughtful, explicitly acknowledging single-center design, selection bias, follow-up heterogeneity, and the correlative nature of mechanistic claims. Some sections could be tightened and a few sentences are awkwardly phrased, but overall readability is good.

key_strengths: Clear prospective-style data collection with blinded CT volumetry and excellent inter-observer agreement (ICC 0.938)
Robust internal validation via bootstrap and 5-fold cross-validation with optimism-corrected C-index of 0.756
Sensitivity analyses for heterogeneous follow-up intervals including mixed-effects modeling and 6-month temporal standardization
Transparent framing of ΔSV as correlative and appropriate positioning of the nomogram for risk stratification rather than treatment decisions
key_concerns: Single-center retrospective design with internally derived optimal cutoff (14%) at risk of overfitting and limited generalizability
No external validation cohort and no prospective confirmation of the nomogram's predictive performance
Absence of peripheral blood or tissue immune profiling means MDSC/Treg mechanistic interpretation remains speculative
Confounding between chemotherapy and immunotherapy effects on splenic volume not disentangled by study design
Data and code not shared; no STROBE checklist referenced and no participant flow diagram in provided text
chief_reviewer.rationale: Competent, well-validated single-center retrospective cohort extending a known radiologic biomarker to gastric cancer immunotherapy; solid internal validation but lacking external validation, mechanistic confirmation, and data sharing places it at tier 3 with minor revisions.
